               Defendants.                                                
11                                                                         

12        In this putative securities class action against Defendant Super Micro Computer, Inc. and 
13   certain of its officers, ten different plaintiff groups have filed motions for appointment as lead 
14   plaintiff.1  Of those, one group has withdrawn its motion,2 and six others have filed statements of 
15   non-opposition.3  The remaining three—Crain Walnut, Universal, and the Covey Investor 
16   Group—filed oppositions to the motions for appointment as lead plaintiff.  Crain Walnut Opp’n, 
17   ECF No. 81; Covey Opp’n, ECF No. 82; Universal Opp’n, ECF No. 83.  However, only Crain 
18   Walnut and Universal filed replies.  Crain Walnut Reply, ECF No. 84; Universal Reply, ECF No. 
19   86.  Thus, it appears that Crain Walnut and Universal are the only two parties actively seeking 
20   appointment as lead plaintiff.                                        
21                                                                         
    1 These ten proposed lead plaintiffs are: (1) Surendra J. Shah; (2) Theodore C. Gross and Theodore 
22   R. Gross (the “Gross Family”); (3) Valikhan Kunakbayev; (4) the Illinois Treasurer; (5) Crain 
    Walnut Shelling, LP; (6) the Public Employees’ Retirement System of Mississippi (“Mississippi 
23   PERS”); (7) Universal-Investment-Gesellschaft mbH; (8) Covey Financial Inc., Pembroke Capital 
    Ltd. Corp., Soverel, Inc., David Burdette, and Priti Bhardwaj (the “Covey Investor Group”); (9) 
24   Erste Asset Management GmbH and Christian Mahé de Berdouaré; and (10) Edward Grosinger, 
    Shmuel Farhi, Robert Hayes, and Deborah Kay Bielss (the “Individual Investor Group”).  Lead 
25   Plf. Mots., ECF Nos. 17, 19, 23, 26, 30, 37, 38, 43, 48, 49.          
26   2 Withdrawal of Mot., ECF No. 77 (Gross Family).                      
    3 Statements of Non-Opp’n, ECF Nos. 74 (Mississippi PERS), 75 (Individual Investor Group), 76 
27   (Erste and Mahé de Berdouaré), 78 (the Illinois Treasurer), 79 (Kunakbayev). 
1        After considering all lead plaintiff papers filed to date, the Court finds that Crain Walnut is 
2   presumptively the lead plaintiff.  However, Universal has raised serious questions raised about 
3   Crain Walnut’s fitness for that role, and further discovery is needed to determine whether 
4   Universal can rebut the presumption that Crain Walnut should be selected as lead plaintiff.  
5   Therefore, the Court ORDERS limited discovery into Crain Walnut and CONTINUES the hearing 
6   on the lead plaintiff motions in this case.                           
7   I.   LEGAL STANDARD                                                   
8        The Private Securities Litigation Reform Act (“PSLRA”), 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4, governs the 
9   selection of lead plaintiffs in securities class actions.  In re Mersho, 6 F.4th 891, 896 (9th Cir. 
10   2021).  Under the PSLRA, courts must “appoint as lead plaintiff the member or members of the 
11   purported plaintiff class that the court determines to be most capable of adequately representing 
12   the interests of class members.”  15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(a)(3)(B)(i).  This does not mean, however, that 
13   courts may conduct “wide-ranging” inquiries into any matter that may bear on a plaintiff’s ability 
14   to serve as lead plaintiff.  In re Cavanaugh, 306 F.3d 726, 729 (9th Cir. 2002).  Rather, the 
15   PSLRA designates as the most capable plaintiff “the one who has the greatest financial stake in the 
16   outcome of the case, so long as he meets the requirements of [Federal Rule of Civil Procedure] 
17   23.”  Id.  To identify a lead plaintiff satisfying the PSLRA’s criteria, courts follow a three-step 
18   process:                                                              
19        First, the plaintiff filing the earliest complaint must publicize basic details about the 
20   proposed securities class action in a widely circulated notice.  Id. (citing 15 U.S.C. § 78u-
21   4(a)(3)(A)).  Any interested plaintiffs must move for appointment as lead plaintiff within sixty 
22   days of the notice’s initial publication.  15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(a)(3)(A)(i)(II). 
23        Second, the court must identify the “presumptively most adequate plaintiff.”  In re 
24   Cavanaugh, 306 F.3d at 730 (citing 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(a)(3)(B)(iii)(I)).  To do that, the court 
25   determines which plaintiff seeking the lead plaintiff position has the highest financial stake in the 
26   litigation.  Id.  Then, turning to that plaintiff’s pleadings and declarations, the court evaluates 
27   whether she has made a prima facie showing that she is typical and adequate under Rule 23(a).  
1   Id.; In re Mersho, 6 F.4th at 899.  If the answer is ‘yes,’ she is presumptively the most adequate 
2   plaintiff.  In re Cavanaugh, 306 F.3d at 730.  If the answer is ‘no,’ the court must move on to the 
3   plaintiff with the next-highest financial stake and repeat its Rule 23(a) analysis.  Id. 
4        Third, other plaintiffs have the chance to rebut the presumption that the plaintiff identified 
5   in the second step is the most adequate.  Id. (citing 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(a)(3)(B)(iii)(II)).  At this 
6   point, the lead plaintiff selection process becomes adversarial, and mere speculation about 
7   adequacy cannot suffice.  In re Mersho, 6 F.4th at 899, 902.  The presumption of adequacy can be 
8   rebutted “only upon proof” that the plaintiff identified in the second step “will not fairly and 
9   adequately protect the interests of the class” or “is subject to unique defenses that render such 
10   plaintiff incapable of adequately representing the class.”  Id. at 899 (quoting 15 U.S.C. § 78u-
11   4(a)(3)(B)(iii)(II)(aa)–(bb)).  If the presumption is not rebutted, the court must select the 
12   presumptively most adequate plaintiff as the lead plaintiff.  Id. (citing 15 U.S.C. § 78u-
13   4(a)(3)(B)(i)).  However, if the presumption is rebutted, the court must return to step two, identify 
14   the plaintiff with the next-highest financial stake, and repeat the process for that plaintiff.  In re 
15   Cavanaugh, 306 F.3d at 731.                                           
16        Of course, at this early stage, plaintiffs will often not have evidence that they can use to 
17   rebut the presumption of adequacy.  To address this issue, the PSLRA authorizes courts to open 
18   limited discovery into the presumptively most adequate plaintiff.  15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(a)(3)(B)(iv).  
19   That said, such discovery is not meant as a tool “to harass presumptive lead plaintiffs.”  In re 
20   Cendant Corp. Litig., 264 F.3d 201, 270 n.49 (3d Cir. 2001).  So, a court may allow discovery only 
21   if a plaintiff challenging the presumption of adequacy “first demonstrates a reasonable basis for a 
22   finding that the presumptively most adequate plaintiff is incapable of adequately representing the 
23   class.”  15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(a)(3)(B)(iv).                              
24   II.  DISCUSSION                                                       
25        A.   Step One                                                    
26        Both Crain Walnut and Universal satisfy the first step of the PSLRA’s lead plaintiff 
27   selection process.  The required PSLRA notice was published on August 30, 2024, Gilmore Decl., 
1   Ex. E, ECF No. 31-5, meaning that any lead plaintiff motions were due on October 29, 2024, sixty 
2   days later.  Crain Walnut and Universal filed their motions by that deadline.  ECF Nos. 30, 38. 
3        B.   Step Two                                                    
4        Since both Crain Walnut and Universal qualify under the PSLRA’s first step, the Court 
5   next evaluates which of the two potential lead plaintiffs is presumptively the most adequate.  Crain 
6   Walnut calculates approximately $49 million in losses from its investment in Super Micro 
7   securities, Gilmore Decl., Ex. B, ECF No. 31-2, which dwarfs Universal’s calculated loss of 
8   approximately $12 million, Uslaner Decl., Ex. B, ECF No. 38-3, as well as every other lead 
9   plaintiff movant’s calculated loss.  Because neither Universal nor any other lead plaintiff movant 
10   meaningfully challenges Crain Walnut’s loss calculation, the Court finds that Crain Walnut has 
11   the largest financial stake.  Accordingly, the Court proceeds to evaluate whether Crain Walnut, 
12   through its pleadings and declarations, has made out a prima facie case that it is adequate and 
13   typical under Rule 23(a).  In re Cavanaugh, 306 F.3d at 730.          
14        A potential lead plaintiff is adequate if it (1) does not have a conflict of interest with the 
15   rest of the class and (2) will vigorously prosecute the action on behalf of the class.  Staton v. 
16   Boeing Co., 327 F.3d 938, 957 (9th Cir. 2003).  That plaintiff is also typical if its claims “are 
17   reasonably co-extensive with those of absent class members.”  DZ Rsrv. v. Meta Platforms, Inc., 
18   96 F.4th 1223, 1238 (9th Cir. 2024) (quoting Hanlon v. Chrysler Corp., 150 F.3d 1011, 1020 (9th 
19   Cir. 1998)).  But a plaintiff “is not typical if ‘there is a danger that absent class members will 
20   suffer if their representative is preoccupied with defenses unique to it.’”  Id. (quoting Hanon v. 
21   Dataproducts Corp., 976 F.2d 497, 508 (9th Cir. 1992)).               
22        Crain Walnut’s declarations and certifications are enough to make a prima facie showing 
23   of adequacy and typicality.  For one, Crain Walnut certified that it purchased Super Micro 
24   securities and suffered losses on those purchases, Certification, ECF No. 31-1, meaning that it is 
25   typical because its claims are co-extensive with those of absent class members.  Crain Walnut also 
26   affirmed that, among other things, it:                                
27          •  did not purchase Super Micro securities at the direction of plaintiff’s counsel or for 
1             the purpose of participating in private securities litigation, Certification ¶ 3; 
2          •  is willing to serve as a representative party, and to provide testimony, id. ¶ 4; 
3          •  reviewed the complaint against Super Micro and authorized filing a lead plaintiff 
4             motion, id. ¶ 2;                                            
5          •  has not served or sought to serve as a lead plaintiff in a securities suit in the past 
6             three years, id. ¶ 6;                                       
7          •  agrees not to accept payment for serving as a representative beyond its pro rata 
8             share of any recovery, except for costs and expenses, id. ¶ 7; 
9          •  understands its duties under the PSLRA, including its duties as a fiduciary for the 
10             class and to oversee counsel and the litigation, Crain Decl. ¶¶ 3, 5–6, 8, ECF No. 
11             31-3;                                                       
12          •  is motivated to and will vigorously prosecute the case, id. ¶¶ 2, 5; and 
13          •  is not aware of any conflicts of interest with the class, or of any unique defenses.  
14             Id. ¶ 11.                                                   
15   These sworn statements make a prima facie showing of adequacy.  Kusen v. Herbert, No. 23-cv-
16   02940-AMO, 2023 WL 8171736, at *4–6 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 24, 2023) (finding that similar sworn 
17   statements established adequacy).                                     
18        Although Universal objects to Crain Walnut’s adequacy on various grounds, none of those 
19   objections affect Crain Walnut’s prima facie showing of typicality and adequacy.  As the Ninth 
20   Circuit made clear, courts assess a potential lead plaintiff’s prima facie case through that 
21   plaintiff’s declarations and pleadings.  In re Cavanaugh, 306 F.3d at 730.  Universal’s objections, 
22   however, are based on information from beyond Crain Walnut’s declarations and pleadings.  They 
23   are not properly considered at the second step of the PSLRA’s lead plaintiff selection process.  
24   Therefore, the Court finds that Crain Walnut is presumptively the most adequate plaintiff.  
25        C.   Step Three                                                  
26        Having found that Crain Walnut is the presumptive lead plaintiff, the Court moves to the 
27   final step of the PSLRA’s selection process.  It is here that the Court evaluates whether 
1   Universal’s arguments against Crain Walnut’s adequacy are enough to rebut the presumption in 
2   favor of Crain Walnut.  The Court concludes that Universal has not rebutted the presumption, but 
3   it has demonstrated a reasonable basis for questioning Crain Walnut’s adequacy.  Therefore, 
4   discovery is necessary before the Court can make a final decision.  See Universal Opp’n 10 
5   (requesting discovery).                                               
6        Universal essentially raises four issues with Crain Walnut’s adequacy: (1) that Crain 
7   Walnut’s opaque corporate structure raises questions about who will be supervising this litigation 
8   if the Court appoints Crain Walnut as lead plaintiff; (2) that Crain Walnut may not be able to 
9   continue as a going concern given its reported $49 million loss on its Super Micro investment; (3) 
10   that Crain Walnut’s decision to invest $144 million over six weeks in a tech stock like Super 
11   Micro raises questions about whether Crain Walnut is a typical investor, see Certification, 
12   especially since Crain Walnut purports to be “in the business of processing, packing and shipping 
13   English Walnut meats,” Crain Decl. ¶ 4; and (4) that the lack of detail about Crain Walnut’s 
14   process for selecting counsel suggests that counsel, rather than Crain Walnut, is driving the 
15   litigation.  The Court addresses each in turn.                        
16        Corporate Structure.  When first moving for appointment as lead plaintiff, Crain Walnut 
17   characterized Charles R. Crain, Jr. (“Mr. Crain”) as its “President, Chief Executive Officer, and 
18   sole owner.”  Certification ¶ 1; see also Crain Decl.  However, as Universal pointed out in 
19   opposition, Crain Walnut is a Delaware limited partnership, and limited partnerships cannot have a 
20   sole owner under Delaware law.  Universal Opp’n 6; see also Del. Code tit. 6, § 17-101(11) 
21   (“‘Limited partnership’ . . . mean[s] a partnership formed under the laws of the State of Delaware 
22   consisting of 2 or more persons and having 1 or more general partners and 1 or more limited 
23   partners . . . .”).  What is more, a search of records filed with the Delaware Secretary of State 
24   revealed Crain Walnut’s general partner to be an entity called Nuez Progresivo, Inc., not Mr. 
25   Crain.  Uslaner Decl., Ex. B, ECF No. 83-3.  In reply, Crain Walnut submitted a supplemental 
26   declaration that further (and more accurately) described its corporate structure.  Crain Walnut 
27   explained that its general partner is Nuez Progresivo, Inc., which is 100% owned by Grupo 
1   Progresivo, Inc., which in turn is 100% owned by Mr. Crain.  Suppl. Crain Decl. ¶ 4, ECF No. 
2   85-1.  Crain Walnut also disclosed that its limited partner is Crain Walnut Shelling, Inc., which is 
3   100% owned by Mr. Crain and for which Mr. Crain serves as the CEO and sole director.  Id.  
4   Based on this, Mr. Crain represents that he effectively has complete control over Crain Walnut 
5   despite its somewhat complicated structure.  Id.                      
6        The problem with this belated clarification is that Crain Walnut had previously held out 
7   Mr. Crain as its “sole owner,” which is technically inconsistent with its actual structure.  There 
8   may well be an innocent reason for this discrepancy—Crain Walnut might have aimed to disclose 
9   who, practically speaking, had decision-making control rather than the specifics of its corporate 
10   structure.  Even if that is so, Crain Walnut’s imprecision at least raises questions about its 
11   carefulness and thoroughness when discussing its corporate structure.  Moreover, Crain Walnut’s 
12   clarification about its partnership structure does not clear up all questions about its corporate 
13   structure.  For instance, Crain Walnut holds itself out “as a division of a large farming business, 
14   Crain Orchards, Inc.”  About Us, Crain Walnut Shelling, LP, https://www.crainwalnut.com/about 
15   [https://perma.cc/5VPX-459L].  That representation appears to be inconsistent with Crain 
16   Walnut’s partnership structure as well.                               
17        None of this proves that Crain Walnut will not adequately supervise counsel, so these 
18   arguments are not enough to rebut the presumption.  But the issues above pose serious questions 
19   about who holds final decision-making authority and how Crain Walnut would oversee this 
20   litigation if appointed as lead plaintiff.  As such, the Court finds that there are reasonable grounds 
21   to open discovery into Crain Walnut’s ownership structure and decision-making processes.  See 
22   Applestein v. Medivation Inc, No. 10-cv-00998-MHP, 2010 WL 3749406, at *5 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 
23   20, 2010) (granting discovery to address “concerns about [a lead plaintiff movant]’s transparency 
24   and its trading practices”); Smajlaj v. Brocade Commc’ns Sys. Inc., No. 05-cv-02042-CRB, 2006 
25   WL 7348107, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 12, 2006) (expressing concern about “continuous ‘new’ 
26   revelations that appear to expose the somewhat complicated and intricate structure of the [lead 
27   plaintiff movant]”).                                                  
1        Going Concern.  Because Crain Walnut is a private company, detailed financial 
2   information is not available.  However, Universal uncovered information from a business data 
3   aggregator estimating Crain Walnut’s annual revenues to be approximately $7.5 million.4  Uslaner 
4   Decl., Ex. A, ECF No. 83-2.  Crain Walnut’s claimed loss of $49 million on its Super Micro 
5   investment is more than six times its estimated annual revenue, calling into question whether 
6   Crain Walnut can bear those losses and continue operating.  Any threat to Crain Walnut’s ability 
7   to continue as a going concern also threatens to interfere with Crain Walnut’s ability to adequately 
8   prosecute this case.                                                  
9        Crain Walnut responds that this revenue estimate is unreliable hearsay and that, instead of 
10   crediting that estimate, the Court should give weight to Mr. Crain’s supplemental declaration 
11   affirming that Crain Walnut is on solid financial footing.  Crain Walnut Reply 6; Suppl. Crain 
12   Decl. ¶ 7.  The Court shares Crain Walnut’s doubts about the reliability of Universal’s proffered 
13   revenue estimate, which is why that estimate, standing alone, is not sufficient to rebut the 
14   presumption of adequacy.  Yet, given the very early stage of this case and Universal’s inability to 
15   access Crain Walnut’s financials, the Court finds that Universal’s revenue estimate is enough to 
16   raise reasonable questions about Crain Walnut’s financial standing, and that there should be 
17   discovery to confirm Crain Walnut’s finances.5                        
18        As an alternative to discovery, Crain Walnut offers to submit financial documents for the 
19   Court to review in camera.  Suppl. Crain Decl. ¶ 7.  While the Court appreciates Crain Walnut’s 
20   willingness to do so, the third step of the lead plaintiff selection process is meant to be 
21                                                                         

22                                                                         
    4 Universal also pointed to another aggregator estimating revenues to be $15.3 million, but that 
23   aggregator appears to be referring to Crain Walnut Shelling, Inc. rather than the limited 
    partnership moving for appointment as lead plaintiff here.  Universal Opp’n 5 (citing Crain 
24   Walnut Shelling Revenue & Competitors, Growjo, https://growjo.com/company/Crain_Walnut_ 
    Shelling [https://perma.cc/GJD8-5P7F]).                               
25   5 Crain Walnut submits other revenue estimates showing that its revenues may be as high as $50 
    million per year.  Crain Walnut Reply 6.  But even crediting those estimates, which all refer to 
26   Crain Walnut Shelling, Inc., Crain Walnut would still have lost a full year’s worth of revenue on 
    its Super Micro investment.  That does not alleviate the concerns about Crain Walnut’s financial 
27   standing.                                                             
1   “adversarial.”  In re Mersho, 6 F.4th at 899.  The PSLRA, too, also calls for competing lead 
2   plaintiff movants to take discovery, not for courts to privately assess evidence.  15 U.S.C. § 78u-
3   4(a)(3)(B)(iv).  The Court will benefit from robust argument by both Crain Walnut and Universal, 
4   so it orders discovery into Crain Walnut’s financial condition rather than in camera submission of 
5   documents.                                                            
6        Typicality.  What most concerns the Court is that much about Crain Walnut’s investment 
7   in Super Micro stock does not add up.  Crain Walnut is purportedly in the business of processing, 
8   packing, and shipping walnuts.  Crain Decl. ¶ 4.  That business, however, is utterly divorced from 
9   Crain Walnut’s $144 million investment into Super Micro, a technology company that provides 
10   server and data storage systems.  Gilmore Decl., Ex. B; Compl. ¶ 20, ECF No. 1.  Although Mr. 
11   Crain later clarified that he uses Crain Walnut “to make investments and generate returns on 
12   money [he has] earned through multiple sources of business and investment income,” Suppl. Crain 
13   Decl. ¶ 7, that only further begs the question why Mr. Crain would choose an entity actively 
14   operating in the walnut market to also serve as his investment vehicle. 
15        Moreover, Crain Walnut amassed its entire $144 million position in Super Micro stock 
16   over the course of six weeks.  Gilmore Decl., Ex. B.  Whether or not pouring this much money 
17   this quickly into a single stock is unusual for large institutional investors, it raises eyebrows when 
18   a walnut company does so.  That being the case, the Court has its doubts about whether Crain 
19   Walnut relied on Super Micro’s alleged misrepresentations to purchase Super Micro stock, like the 
20   typical class member, or of some other reason might have driven Crain Walnut’s decision to 
21   rapidly acquire stock.  See Marjanian v. Allied Nev. Gold Corp., No. 2:14-cv-0650-JCM-VCF, 
22   2014 WL 12769810, at *7–8 (D. Nev. Nov. 7, 2014) (noting that reliance issues might render a 
23   potential lead plaintiff atypical).                                   
24        Accordingly, the Court also allows discovery into the circumstances of Crain Walnut’s 
25   purchase of Super Micro stock.                                        
26        Selection of Counsel.  Finally, Universal questions Crain Walnut’s selection of counsel.  
27   But Universal’s argument is largely based on the fact that Crain Walnut did not provide more 
1   detail about its counsel selection process.  In attempting to argue from lack of detail, Universal 
2   speculates about what might have caused Crain Walnut to select its counsel.  That speculation is 
3   certainly not the “proof” required to rebut the presumption of adequacy.  See 15 U.S.C. § 78u-
4   4(a)(3)(B)(iii)(II).  Nor is it enough to establish a reasonable basis for discovery.  See 15 U.S.C. 
5   § 78u-4(a)(3)(B)(iv).  So, the Court does not permit discovery into Crain Walnut’s choice of 
6   counsel.                                                              
7   III.  CONCLUSION                                                      
8        In sum, the Court finds that Crain Walnut is the presumptively most adequate plaintiff, but 
9   that Universal has raised a reasonable basis for conducting further discovery into Crain Walnut.  
10   The Court therefore GRANTS discovery into Crain Walnut’s suitability for the role of lead 
11   plaintiff, limited to the topics identified as appropriate for discovery in this Order.  Crain Walnut 
12   and Universal shall proceed with discovery as follows:                
13          •  Discovery shall remain open for sixty (60) days;            
14          •  Within ten (10) days of this Order, Crain Walnut and Universal shall submit a 
15             protective order for Court approval;                        
16          •  Due to the abbreviated time for conducting discovery, Crain Walnut must respond 
17             to discovery requests within twenty-one (21) days of service; 
18          •  Crain Walnut and Universal must meet and confer via live communication 
19             regarding any discovery disputes before seeking Court intervention; 
20          •  Any discovery motions must be filed within fourteen (14) days of service of 
21             objections.                                                 
22        To allow time for discovery, the Court CONTINUES the upcoming hearing on lead 
23   plaintiff selection, currently scheduled for December 19, 2024 at 9:00 am, to March 6, 2025 at 
24   9:00 am.  At least fourteen (14) days before the hearing, Crain Walnut and Universal shall file 
25   supplemental briefs of no more than fifteen (15) pages addressing the discovery into Crain 
26   Walnut.  Because both parties will have a chance to file supplemental briefs, the Court also 
27   DENIES Universal’s motion for leave to file a sur-reply.  ECF No. 91.  Universal can make any 
    1    argument in its supplemental brief that it wanted to make in its proposed sur-reply. 
    2          IT IS SO ORDERED. 
    3    Dated: December 12, 2024 
    4 
    5 
                                                        EDWARD J. DAVILA 
    6                                                    United States District Judge

306 F.3d 726
, 729 (9th Cir. 2002).  Rather, the 
15   PSLRA designates as the most capable plaintiff “the one who has the greatest financial stake in the 
16   outcome of the case, so long as he meets the requirements of [Federal Rule of Civil Procedure] 
17   23.”  Id.  To identify a lead plaintiff satisfying the PSLRA’s criteria, courts follow a three-step 
18   process:                                                              
19        First, the plaintiff filing the earliest complaint must publicize basic details about the 
20   proposed securities class action in a widely circulated notice.  Id. (citing 15 U.S.C. § 78u-
21   4(a)(3)(A)).  Any interested plaintiffs must move for appointment as lead plaintiff within sixty 
22   days of the notice’s initial publication.  15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(a)(3)(A)(i)(II). 
23        Second, the court must identify the “presumptively most adequate plaintiff.”  In re 
24   Cavanaugh, 306 F.3d at 730 (citing 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(a)(3)(B)(iii)(I)).  To do that, the court 
25   determines which plaintiff seeking the lead plaintiff position has the highest financial stake in the 
26   litigation.  Id.  Then, turning to that plaintiff’s pleadings and declarations, the court evaluates 
27   whether she has made a prima facie showing that she is typical and adequate under Rule 23(a).  
1   Id.; In re Mersho, 6 F.4th at 899.  If the answer is ‘yes,’ she is presumptively the most adequate 
2   plaintiff.  In re Cavanaugh, 306 F.3d at 730.  If the answer is ‘no,’ the court must move on to the 
3   plaintiff with the next-highest financial stake and repeat its Rule 23(a) analysis.  Id. 
4        Third, other plaintiffs have the chance to rebut the presumption that the plaintiff identified 
5   in the second step is the most adequate.  Id. (citing 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(a)(3)(B)(iii)(II)).  At this 
6   point, the lead plaintiff selection process becomes adversarial, and mere speculation about 
7   adequacy cannot suffice.  In re Mersho, 6 F.4th at 899, 902.  The presumption of adequacy can be 
8   rebutted “only upon proof” that the plaintiff identified in the second step “will not fairly and 
9   adequately protect the interests of the class” or “is subject to unique defenses that render such 
10   plaintiff incapable of adequately representing the class.”  Id. at 899 (quoting 15 U.S.C. § 78u-
11   4(a)(3)(B)(iii)(II)(aa)–(bb)).  If the presumption is not rebutted, the court must select the 
12   presumptively most adequate plaintiff as the lead plaintiff.  Id. (citing 15 U.S.C. § 78u-
13   4(a)(3)(B)(i)).  However, if the presumption is rebutted, the court must return to step two, identify 
14   the plaintiff with the next-highest financial stake, and repeat the process for that plaintiff.  In re 
15   Cavanaugh, 306 F.3d at 731.                                           
16        Of course, at this early stage, plaintiffs will often not have evidence that they can use to 
17   rebut the presumption of adequacy.  To address this issue, the PSLRA authorizes courts to open 
18   limited discovery into the presumptively most adequate plaintiff.  15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(a)(3)(B)(iv).  
19   That said, such discovery is not meant as a tool “to harass presumptive lead plaintiffs.”  In re 
20   Cendant Corp. Litig.,
264 F.3d 201
, 270 n.49 (3d Cir. 2001).  So, a court may allow discovery only 
21   if a plaintiff challenging the presumption of adequacy “first demonstrates a reasonable basis for a 
22   finding that the presumptively most adequate plaintiff is incapable of adequately representing the 
23   class.”  15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(a)(3)(B)(iv).                              
24   II.  DISCUSSION                                                       
25        A.   Step One                                                    
26        Both Crain Walnut and Universal satisfy the first step of the PSLRA’s lead plaintiff 
27   selection process.  The required PSLRA notice was published on August 30, 2024, Gilmore Decl., 
1   Ex. E, ECF No. 31-5, meaning that any lead plaintiff motions were due on October 29, 2024, sixty 
2   days later.  Crain Walnut and Universal filed their motions by that deadline.  ECF Nos. 30, 38. 
3        B.   Step Two                                                    
4        Since both Crain Walnut and Universal qualify under the PSLRA’s first step, the Court 
5   next evaluates which of the two potential lead plaintiffs is presumptively the most adequate.  Crain 
6   Walnut calculates approximately $49 million in losses from its investment in Super Micro 
7   securities, Gilmore Decl., Ex. B, ECF No. 31-2, which dwarfs Universal’s calculated loss of 
8   approximately $12 million, Uslaner Decl., Ex. B, ECF No. 38-3, as well as every other lead 
9   plaintiff movant’s calculated loss.  Because neither Universal nor any other lead plaintiff movant 
10   meaningfully challenges Crain Walnut’s loss calculation, the Court finds that Crain Walnut has 
11   the largest financial stake.  Accordingly, the Court proceeds to evaluate whether Crain Walnut, 
12   through its pleadings and declarations, has made out a prima facie case that it is adequate and 
13   typical under Rule 23(a).  In re Cavanaugh, 306 F.3d at 730.          
14        A potential lead plaintiff is adequate if it (1) does not have a conflict of interest with the 
15   rest of the class and (2) will vigorously prosecute the action on behalf of the class.  Staton v. 
16   Boeing Co.,
327 F.3d 938, 957
 (9th Cir. 2003).  That plaintiff is also typical if its claims “are 
17   reasonably co-extensive with those of absent class members.”  DZ Rsrv. v. Meta Platforms, Inc., 
18
96 F.4th 1223
, 1238 (9th Cir. 2024) (quoting Hanlon v. Chrysler Corp.,
150 F.3d 1011, 1020
 (9th 
19   Cir. 1998)).  But a plaintiff “is not typical if ‘there is a danger that absent class members will 
20   suffer if their representative is preoccupied with defenses unique to it.’”
Id.
 (quoting Hanon v. 
21   Dataproducts Corp.,
976 F.2d 497, 508
 (9th Cir. 1992)).               
22        Crain Walnut’s declarations and certifications are enough to make a prima facie showing 
23   of adequacy and typicality.  For one, Crain Walnut certified that it purchased Super Micro 
24   securities and suffered losses on those purchases, Certification, ECF No. 31-1, meaning that it is 
25   typical because its claims are co-extensive with those of absent class members.  Crain Walnut also 
26   affirmed that, among other things, it:                                
27          •  did not purchase Super Micro securities at the direction of plaintiff’s counsel or for 
1             the purpose of participating in private securities litigation, Certification ¶ 3; 
2          •  is willing to serve as a representative party, and to provide testimony, id. ¶ 4; 
3          •  reviewed the complaint against Super Micro and authorized filing a lead plaintiff 
4             motion, id. ¶ 2;                                            
5          •  has not served or sought to serve as a lead plaintiff in a securities suit in the past 
6             three years, id. ¶ 6;                                       
7          •  agrees not to accept payment for serving as a representative beyond its pro rata 
8             share of any recovery, except for costs and expenses, id. ¶ 7; 
9          •  understands its duties under the PSLRA, including its duties as a fiduciary for the 
10             class and to oversee counsel and the litigation, Crain Decl. ¶¶ 3, 5–6, 8, ECF No. 
11             31-3;                                                       
12          •  is motivated to and will vigorously prosecute the case, id. ¶¶ 2, 5; and 
13          •  is not aware of any conflicts of interest with the class, or of any unique defenses.  
14             Id. ¶ 11.                                                   
15   These sworn statements make a prima facie showing of adequacy.  Kusen v. Herbert, No. 23-cv-
16   02940-AMO,
2023 WL 8171736
, at *4–6 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 24, 2023) (finding that similar sworn 
17   statements established adequacy).                                     
18        Although Universal objects to Crain Walnut’s adequacy on various grounds, none of those 
19   objections affect Crain Walnut’s prima facie showing of typicality and adequacy.  As the Ninth 
20   Circuit made clear, courts assess a potential lead plaintiff’s prima facie case through that 
21   plaintiff’s declarations and pleadings.  In re Cavanaugh, 306 F.3d at 730.  Universal’s objections, 
22   however, are based on information from beyond Crain Walnut’s declarations and pleadings.  They 
23   are not properly considered at the second step of the PSLRA’s lead plaintiff selection process.  
24   Therefore, the Court finds that Crain Walnut is presumptively the most adequate plaintiff.  
25        C.   Step Three                                                  
26        Having found that Crain Walnut is the presumptive lead plaintiff, the Court moves to the 
27   final step of the PSLRA’s selection process.  It is here that the Court evaluates whether 
1   Universal’s arguments against Crain Walnut’s adequacy are enough to rebut the presumption in 
2   favor of Crain Walnut.  The Court concludes that Universal has not rebutted the presumption, but 
3   it has demonstrated a reasonable basis for questioning Crain Walnut’s adequacy.  Therefore, 
4   discovery is necessary before the Court can make a final decision.  See Universal Opp’n 10 
5   (requesting discovery).                                               
6        Universal essentially raises four issues with Crain Walnut’s adequacy: (1) that Crain 
7   Walnut’s opaque corporate structure raises questions about who will be supervising this litigation 
8   if the Court appoints Crain Walnut as lead plaintiff; (2) that Crain Walnut may not be able to 
9   continue as a going concern given its reported $49 million loss on its Super Micro investment; (3) 
10   that Crain Walnut’s decision to invest $144 million over six weeks in a tech stock like Super 
11   Micro raises questions about whether Crain Walnut is a typical investor, see Certification, 
12   especially since Crain Walnut purports to be “in the business of processing, packing and shipping 
13   English Walnut meats,” Crain Decl. ¶ 4; and (4) that the lack of detail about Crain Walnut’s 
14   process for selecting counsel suggests that counsel, rather than Crain Walnut, is driving the 
15   litigation.  The Court addresses each in turn.                        
16        Corporate Structure.  When first moving for appointment as lead plaintiff, Crain Walnut 
17   characterized Charles R. Crain, Jr. (“Mr. Crain”) as its “President, Chief Executive Officer, and 
18   sole owner.”  Certification ¶ 1; see also Crain Decl.  However, as Universal pointed out in 
19   opposition, Crain Walnut is a Delaware limited partnership, and limited partnerships cannot have a 
20   sole owner under Delaware law.  Universal Opp’n 6; see also Del. Code tit. 6, § 17-101(11) 
21   (“‘Limited partnership’ . . . mean[s] a partnership formed under the laws of the State of Delaware 
22   consisting of 2 or more persons and having 1 or more general partners and 1 or more limited 
23   partners . . . .”).  What is more, a search of records filed with the Delaware Secretary of State 
24   revealed Crain Walnut’s general partner to be an entity called Nuez Progresivo, Inc., not Mr. 
25   Crain.  Uslaner Decl., Ex. B, ECF No. 83-3.  In reply, Crain Walnut submitted a supplemental 
26   declaration that further (and more accurately) described its corporate structure.  Crain Walnut 
27   explained that its general partner is Nuez Progresivo, Inc., which is 100% owned by Grupo 
1   Progresivo, Inc., which in turn is 100% owned by Mr. Crain.  Suppl. Crain Decl. ¶ 4, ECF No. 
2   85-1.  Crain Walnut also disclosed that its limited partner is Crain Walnut Shelling, Inc., which is 
3   100% owned by Mr. Crain and for which Mr. Crain serves as the CEO and sole director.  Id.  
4   Based on this, Mr. Crain represents that he effectively has complete control over Crain Walnut 
5   despite its somewhat complicated structure.  Id.                      
6        The problem with this belated clarification is that Crain Walnut had previously held out 
7   Mr. Crain as its “sole owner,” which is technically inconsistent with its actual structure.  There 
8   may well be an innocent reason for this discrepancy—Crain Walnut might have aimed to disclose 
9   who, practically speaking, had decision-making control rather than the specifics of its corporate 
10   structure.  Even if that is so, Crain Walnut’s imprecision at least raises questions about its 
11   carefulness and thoroughness when discussing its corporate structure.  Moreover, Crain Walnut’s 
12   clarification about its partnership structure does not clear up all questions about its corporate 
13   structure.  For instance, Crain Walnut holds itself out “as a division of a large farming business, 
14   Crain Orchards, Inc.”  About Us, Crain Walnut Shelling, LP, https://www.crainwalnut.com/about 
15   [https://perma.cc/5VPX-459L].  That representation appears to be inconsistent with Crain 
16   Walnut’s partnership structure as well.                               
17        None of this proves that Crain Walnut will not adequately supervise counsel, so these 
18   arguments are not enough to rebut the presumption.  But the issues above pose serious questions 
19   about who holds final decision-making authority and how Crain Walnut would oversee this 
20   litigation if appointed as lead plaintiff.  As such, the Court finds that there are reasonable grounds 
21   to open discovery into Crain Walnut’s ownership structure and decision-making processes.  See 
22   Applestein v. Medivation Inc, No. 10-cv-00998-MHP,
2010 WL 3749406
, at *5 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 
23   20, 2010) (granting discovery to address “concerns about [a lead plaintiff movant]’s transparency 
24   and its trading practices”); Smajlaj v. Brocade Commc’ns Sys. Inc., No. 05-cv-02042-CRB, 2006
25 WL 7348107
, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 12, 2006) (expressing concern about “continuous ‘new’ 
26   revelations that appear to expose the somewhat complicated and intricate structure of the [lead 
27   plaintiff movant]”).                                                  
1        Going Concern.  Because Crain Walnut is a private company, detailed financial 
2   information is not available.  However, Universal uncovered information from a business data 
3   aggregator estimating Crain Walnut’s annual revenues to be approximately $7.5 million.4  Uslaner 
4   Decl., Ex. A, ECF No. 83-2.  Crain Walnut’s claimed loss of $49 million on its Super Micro 
5   investment is more than six times its estimated annual revenue, calling into question whether 
6   Crain Walnut can bear those losses and continue operating.  Any threat to Crain Walnut’s ability 
7   to continue as a going concern also threatens to interfere with Crain Walnut’s ability to adequately 
8   prosecute this case.                                                  
9        Crain Walnut responds that this revenue estimate is unreliable hearsay and that, instead of 
10   crediting that estimate, the Court should give weight to Mr. Crain’s supplemental declaration 
11   affirming that Crain Walnut is on solid financial footing.  Crain Walnut Reply 6; Suppl. Crain 
12   Decl. ¶ 7.  The Court shares Crain Walnut’s doubts about the reliability of Universal’s proffered 
13   revenue estimate, which is why that estimate, standing alone, is not sufficient to rebut the 
14   presumption of adequacy.  Yet, given the very early stage of this case and Universal’s inability to 
15   access Crain Walnut’s financials, the Court finds that Universal’s revenue estimate is enough to 
16   raise reasonable questions about Crain Walnut’s financial standing, and that there should be 
17   discovery to confirm Crain Walnut’s finances.5                        
18        As an alternative to discovery, Crain Walnut offers to submit financial documents for the 
19   Court to review in camera.  Suppl. Crain Decl. ¶ 7.  While the Court appreciates Crain Walnut’s 
20   willingness to do so, the third step of the lead plaintiff selection process is meant to be

6        Typicality.  What most concerns the Court is that much about Crain Walnut’s investment 
7   in Super Micro stock does not add up.  Crain Walnut is purportedly in the business of processing, 
8   packing, and shipping walnuts.  Crain Decl. ¶ 4.  That business, however, is utterly divorced from 
9   Crain Walnut’s $144 million investment into Super Micro, a technology company that provides 
10   server and data storage systems.  Gilmore Decl., Ex. B; Compl. ¶ 20, ECF No. 1.  Although Mr. 
11   Crain later clarified that he uses Crain Walnut “to make investments and generate returns on 
12   money [he has] earned through multiple sources of business and investment income,” Suppl. Crain 
13   Decl. ¶ 7, that only further begs the question why Mr. Crain would choose an entity actively 
14   operating in the walnut market to also serve as his investment vehicle. 
15        Moreover, Crain Walnut amassed its entire $144 million position in Super Micro stock 
16   over the course of six weeks.  Gilmore Decl., Ex. B.  Whether or not pouring this much money 
17   this quickly into a single stock is unusual for large institutional investors, it raises eyebrows when 
18   a walnut company does so.  That being the case, the Court has its doubts about whether Crain 
19   Walnut relied on Super Micro’s alleged misrepresentations to purchase Super Micro stock, like the 
20   typical class member, or of some other reason might have driven Crain Walnut’s decision to 
21   rapidly acquire stock.  See Marjanian v. Allied Nev. Gold Corp., No. 2:14-cv-0650-JCM-VCF, 
22
2014 WL 12769810
, at *7–8 (D. Nev. Nov. 7, 2014) (noting that reliance issues might render a 
23   potential lead plaintiff atypical).                                   
24        Accordingly, the Court also allows discovery into the circumstances of Crain Walnut’s 
25   purchase of Super Micro stock.                                        
26        Selection of Counsel.  Finally, Universal questions Crain Walnut’s selection of counsel.  
27   But Universal’s argument is largely based on the fact that Crain Walnut did not provide more 
1   detail about its counsel selection process.  In attempting to argue from lack of detail, Universal 
2   speculates about what might have caused Crain Walnut to select its counsel.  That speculation is 
3   certainly not the “proof” required to rebut the presumption of adequacy.  See 15 U.S.C. § 78u-
4   4(a)(3)(B)(iii)(II).  Nor is it enough to establish a reasonable basis for discovery.  See 15 U.S.C. 
5   § 78u-4(a)(3)(B)(iv).  So, the Court does not permit discovery into Crain Walnut’s choice of 
6   counsel.                                                              
7   III.  CONCLUSION                                                      
8        In sum, the Court finds that Crain Walnut is the presumptively most adequate plaintiff, but 
9   that Universal has raised a reasonable basis for conducting further discovery into Crain Walnut.  
10   The Court therefore GRANTS discovery into Crain Walnut’s suitability for the role of lead 
11   plaintiff, limited to the topics identified as appropriate for discovery in this Order.  Crain Walnut 
12   and Universal shall proceed with discovery as follows:
